Insights into the physicochemical properties of newly synthesized benzyl triethylammonium chloride-based deep eutectic solvents

ABSTRACT In order to utilize deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as a replacement for conventional organic solvents for different applications, a detailed understanding of their physicochemical properties is extremely important. In this study, several novel DESs based on benzyl-triethylammonium chloride (BTEA) as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and acids/or alcohols as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) have been synthesized. DESs have been thoroughly characterized and investigated for their physicochemical properties viz. thermal stability, glass transition temperature, viscosity (η), surface tension (γ), refractive index (nD), density (ρ), speed of sound (u), and conductivity (κ) in a temperature range of 293.15–343.15 K. The effect of temperature, type of HBDs, and alkyl chain length of HBDs of the DESs on the physicochemical properties are critically examined and discussed. Viscosity data are fitted to Vogel-Fulcher-Tamman (VFT) and Arrhenius models. A linear model was used to fit surface tension (γ), density, refractive index, and speed of sound data whereas conductivity data were fitted to a nonlinear equation. Primary data on physicochemical properties have been used to estimate the viscous flow parameters (activation entropy, activation enthalpy, and free energy of activation) and other derived parameters such as lattice energy, standard entropy, molar volume, intermolecular free length, and isentropic compressibility. A relationship between molar conductivity and dynamic viscosity has been established to evaluate the ionicity of the synthesized DESs. Insights into the structure–property correlations are discussed in detail.

## 1. Introduction Organic solvents, which are highly combustible, poisonous, and hazardous to the environment as well as to human health, are one of the main and most frequent sources of chemicals and industrial processes. To meet the requirements of green chemistry principles, new ecologically friendly and sustainable solvents must be developed [1]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are well known for being the new adaptable, environmentally friendly, and designer solvents that can be easily created by merely combining the HBDs and HBAs in a specific molar ratio. The melting temperature of the generated liquid will be lesser than the melting points of their individual HBAs and HBDs. Abbott et al. published DESs for the very first time by mixing choline chloride (ChCl) as (HBA) and urea as (HBD) in 2003 [2]. The development of DESs depends on several interactions, including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals interaction, non-symmetricity, and mixing entropy. Even at high

temperatures, several of the DESs combinations show chemical and thermal stability, with no chemical changes in their properties [3]. DESs can overcome the limitations associated with organic solvents by pos-sessing good thermal stability, low vapor pressure, non-flammability, large liquidus range, and biodegradability [4]. Although DESs are sometimes referred to as a class of ionic liquids, they differ from ionic liquids in some ways, including being less hazardous, not requiring purification, and being simpler to synthesize, which makes them easier to scale up for large-scale manufacturing [5]. DESs can have either a hydrophilic or a hydrophobic character, depending on the makeup of the constituent parts. Long-chain alkyl groups typically cause an increase in hydrophobicity. For a long time, the potential of hydrophilic DESs has been investigated in a variety of disciplines, including biomass extrac-tion, and processing, catalysis, enzyme activation, nanomaterials syn-thesis, gas separation, electrodeposition, battery technology, and pharmaceutical, etc [6–11]. When designing process equipment and scaling it up, an engineer must have a thorough understanding of thermophysical parameters connected to the solvent, such as density, viscosity, and refractive index. Pumping, mixing, and equipment size are all impacted by these characteristics, as well as mass and heat transmission. Data on thermophysical properties are also useful in choosing solvents that are appropriate for a certain procedure [15]. To better understand these characteristics of DESs, the scientific community is contributing its finest work. Accordingly, Soares et al. [16] investigated the density, viscosity, and Kamlet-Taft parameters of sodium hexanoate and decanoate-based eutectic solvents at a temperature range of 293.15–353.15 K. In the same temperature range of 293.15–343.15 K, Sánchez et al. [17] tested several additional physical characteristics, including refractive index, speed of sound, thermal expansion coefficient, isentropic-compressibility of proline and betaine-based DESs. To comprehend the fundamentals better, Achkar et al. [18] successfully wrapped up a discussion of several of these physical characteristics of DESs systems. Abbott et al. [2] measured the viscosity, refractive index, surface tension, and conductivity of [Ch]Cl: urea, and those of [Ch][Cl]: mono (phenylacetic, phenyl propionic), di (oxalic, malonic, adipic, and succinic), and tri (citric) acids [19], as well as the density, viscosity, conductivity, and surface tensions of [Ch]: ethylene glycol, glycerol, 1,4 butane diol [20]. The DESs [Ch]Cl: ethylene glycol and [Ch]Cl: glycerol, and their aqueous solutions, were measured between 298.15 and 333.15 K by Leron et al. [21] To evaluate the densities of nine distinct salts, Shahbaz et al. [22] utilized various HBAs such as methyl triphenylphosphonium, cholinium, and N-N, diethyl ethanolammonium, with numerous HBDs, including ethylene glycol, 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, and glycerol. It is also important to emphasize the work of Biernacki et al. [23]. They studied the type III DESs composed of xylitol, and sorbitol with choline chloride via experimental and computational approaches. In temperatures ranging from 293.15 to 353.15 K, researchers have studied the physicochemical characteristics of these DESs, including their density, viscosity, electrical conductivity, molar volume, refractive index, and molar refraction. Gardas and colleagues designed a new series of DESs by selecting benzyl tripropylammonium as HBA with lactic acid, phenol, glycerol, and ethylene glycol as HBDs. Several distinct thermodynamic parameters such as density, speed of sound, conductivity, and refractive index have been determined in the temperature range of 293.15 K–343.15 K [24]. In their expanded work reports, the same research group provide a new series of DES by replacing their previous HBA with current benzyl trimethylammonium chloride and benzyl tributylammonium chloride as HBAs with previously used HBDs. They carefully evaluated the characteristics of each DESs, such as density, sound speed, viscosity, refractive index, and electrical conductivity, and found that the molar ratio of HBD/HBA significantly affected the physicochemical characteristics of DESs in the temperature range of 283.15–343.15 K [25].

Herein, we have performed synthesis, characterization, and detailed physicochemical study of these newly synthesized DESs utilizing benzyl triethylammonium chloride (BTEA) as HBA with various organic acids (formic, acetic, butyric, valeric, pivalic, caprylic, capric, lauric, oleic, lactic, and levulinic acid) and alcohols (propane 1,2 diol, butane 1, 4 diol, and ethylene glycol) as HBDs. Investigations have been done into how several conditions, including temperature, alkyl chain length, and HBD type affect these physical properties. Physicochemical insights have been gained through precise measurements of primary physical properties such as viscosity, surface tension, refractive index, density, speed of sound, conductivity, and derived properties such as activation parameters of viscous flow (AH*, AS*, and AG*), molar volume, lattice energy, standard entropy, intermolecular free length, and isentropic
compressibility as a function of temperature (293.15–343.15) at atmo- spheric pressure. Correlations of viscosity and conductivity have also been evaluated and presented.

2.2.2. Physicochemical characterization All the synthesized DESs underwent thermogravimetric analysis using the Mettler Toledo Star SW 8.10 system in a nitrogen environment and at a rate of 5 °C/min, and DSC analysis by Phoenix DSC 204 F1 instrument with 10 °C rise per minute. Viscosity measurements for all the synthesized DESs were carried out using an Anton Paar Dynamic Viscosity: AMVn Automated Micro Viscometer (relative standard uncertainty 0.01). The Attention Sigma 700 (relative standard uncertainty 0.1) was used to measure the surface tension. Anton Paar (Model DSA 5000) vibrating tube density meter was used to measure the density (relative standard uncertainty of 0.005), and speed of sound (relative standard uncertainty of 0.001). Refractive indices have been recorded using a Mettler-Toledo (Model RE-40 D) refractometer (relative standard uncertainty 0.0001) with a high-resolution optical sensor. Conductivity (κ) measurements were performed using a Thermo Scientific™ Eutech™ PC 2700 Multi-parameter Meter with pH Electrode (ECFG73711B), Conductivity Electrode (CONSEN921D), and ATC Probe (PH5TEMB1P) (relative standard uncertainty 0.02).

## 3. Result and discussion ### 3.1. *Thermal Stability, and glass transition temperature determination* To ascertain the thermal stability of the synthesized DESs in terms of decomposition temperature, *T*d, a thermogravimetric study was carried

out. Fig. 2 shows the thermogram of newly synthesized DESs whereas the thermal stability of remaining earlier synthesized DESs is reported in our previous article [5]. Table 2 includes the associated degradation temperature for each DESs. It can be clearly observed that all the synthesized DESs show a good thermal stability range from 453.15 to 498.15 K. The observed thermal stability of DESs is showing comparable results with the previous findings [26]. Increasing chain length has been found to increase the viscosity, and DESs with higher viscosities have greater thermal stability [25]. Here, DESs with acids having comparatively smaller molecules such as BTEA: FA, BTEA: AA, BTEA: BA, BTEA: VA, and BTEA: PA has little effect on the thermal stability whereas, a significant increase in thermal stability has been observed for acids of significant chain length with increase in chain length such as BTEA: CAP (453.15 K), BTEA: CA (471.15 K), BTEA: LAU (478.15 K), and BTEA: OLE (498.15 K). This pattern is also seen in other DESs, such as BTEA: LA (473.15 K), BTEA: PRO (468.15 K), which exhibit less thermal stability than BTEA: LEV (478.15 K), and BTEA: BUT (498.15 K).

One of the most noteworthy qualities in DESs, in addition to the decomposition temperature, is the melting temperature, particularly when used to replace standard solvents. The range of temperatures where DESs can maintain their liquid state depends on these features. The melting point of the mixture has been consistently demonstrated to be lower than that of its constituent parts, making it impossible for DSC to detect most DESs. Instead, each DES displayed a glass transition temperature, proving that these DESs are supramolecular complexes capable of existing in a liquid state over a wide temperature range [45]. Additionally, the hydrogen bonds formed by the HBA and HBDs also serve to shield anion from cation, reducing electrostatic interaction and, ultimately, melting point [46]. 3.2. *Viscosity* To describe the solvent's mobility and flow resistance, viscosity is an important physical property. It is also critical to research how temperature impacts DESs viscosity to judge their utility and calculate the

energy required to process them [27]. Fig. 3a illustrates the experi- mental fluctuations in viscosities of all the synthesized DESs with tem- peratures ranging from 293.15 K to 343.15 K at 5 K intervals. The plot clearly shows that, as would be predicted, viscosities appear to be dropping exponentially as the temperature rises. The Hole Theory, which governs the mobility of species into mixtures, can be used to explain temperature effects. When the DESs mixture is heated, addi- tional energy is added, which speeds up and spreads out molecules, creating large holes that allow molecules to pass each other with ease and subsequently reduce viscosity [28]. The experimental viscosity data of the DESs are summarized in Table S1. The Vogel-Fulcher-Tamman (VFT) model and Arrhenius model are the two models that are most frequently used to analyze how temperature affects viscosity in DESs.

In addition to the impact of temperature, chain length has an important function. It was found that when the molecular weight of the various DESs increased, so did their viscosities. This pattern is consistent with the Mark-Houwink equation, which is frequently used to characterize the viscosity behavior of polymers [32]. Thus, as chain length rises, the molecular weight tends to rise as well, increasing viscosity. As a result, The BTEA: FA DES corresponds to lower viscosity among all the studied acidic DESs at lower (293.15 K, 514.469 mPa.s) as well as at higher temperatures (353.15 K, 24.625 mPa.s) due to its shorter chain length. Sarmad et al. [33] evaluated the viscosity of various DESs for screening towards green CO2 sorbent. From there, our measured results are in good agreement with previously reported values for the dynamic viscosity of one of the DESs (BTEA: AA) that was the subject of this investigation. In addition to temperature and chain length, the viscosity is also dependent upon the nature of HBDs [34]. A similar tendency of increased viscosity has also been noted when acids are replaced by alcohol. Because of this BTEA: EG (411.478 mPa.s) is having a lower viscosity than BTEA: PRO (828.389 mPa.s), and BTEA: BUT (834.398 mPa.s) at 293.15 K.

3.2.1. The association activation parameters studied for all DESs It is also important to define the operational settings for the process after acquiring experimental viscosity data. Then, because viscosity is a direct result of intermolecular interactions, it can offer information on a molecular basis. Determining thermodynamic activation parameters of viscous flow using the Eyring equation is one of the methods for understanding intermolecular interactions from viscosity [35]. The associated activation parameters for their viscous flow, namely ΔH* (enthalpy of activation), ΔG* (free energy of activation), and ΔS* (entropy of activation), have been earlier analyzed for various ionic liquids [36,37]. Considering the energy of activation (ΔG*), which is identical to the enthalpy of activation, (ΔH*). The Arrhenius version of viscosity relations can be expressed as,
$\eta = \left(\frac{hN_A}{V_m}\right) e^{\frac{\Delta H^{\ddagger}}{RT}} e^{-\frac{\Delta S^{\ddagger}}{k}}$ (3)

Where h is Planck's constant in J.s, NA is Avogadro's number (mol⁻¹), R is the gas constant (8.314 JK⁻¹mol⁻¹) and Vm is the molar volume in m³ mol⁻¹. Taking the logarithm of the above equation, we get
$$ln\eta = \left\{ \ln\left(\frac{hN_A}{V_m}\right) - \frac{\Delta S^*}{R} \right\} + \frac{\Delta H^*}{RT}\tag{4}$$

The calculated values of activation parameters (ΔG*, ΔH*, and ΔS*) is represented in Tables S3–S5. The behavior of these activation pa- rameters concerning temperature is shown in Fig. 4. The process is assumed to be non-spontaneous since the viscous flow is confronted by the activation barrier, as shown by the positive values of ΔG*. The Gibbs free energy values are falling with increasing temperature, indicating that less energy is required to initiate viscous flows as shown in Fig. 4a. It is interesting to note that as the chain length grows, more energy is needed to start the viscous flow. 4. Conclusions This work effectively synthesized 14 distinct DESs (including hy-drophilic as well as hydrophobic) by using benzyl triethylammonium chloride as HBA with several acids and alcohols as HBDs. Synthesized DESs are showing good thermal stability in the temperature range of 453.15–498.15 K and free-flowing ability. Physical and derived prop-erties have been analyzed as a function of temperature and structure. It has been found that as the temperature rises viscosity decreases and conductivity increases non-linearly whereas other properties such as density, surface tension, refractive index, and sound speed show a linear downward trend. The data for molar volume, intermolecular free length, isentropic compressibility, and standard entropy showed an upward trend with temperature. No appreciable variation in hardcore molecular volumes was found with the rise in temperature whereas an increase in the free volume of DESs was observed with the temperature rise. Vis-cosity measurements show the viscoelastic nature of DESs. Physical properties were also found to be significantly influenced by the change in the molecular weight/chain length of components of various DESs. The surface tension of DESs containing alcohols was higher than that of DESs based on acids, which may be related to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBA and alcohols, whereas the density of benzyl tri (alkyl) ammonium chloride-based DESs having the same HBD decreases in the order methyl > ethyl > propyl > butyl and single acid-based DESs displayed a lower density value than the double acid-based DESs. Interestingly, hydrophilic DESs are denser than water while hydrophobic DESs have lower density as compared to water. Conductivity and viscosity correlation reveals that the synthesized DESs are subionic in character wherein hydrophobic DESs are less ionic as compared to hydrophilic DESs. In a nutshell, the studies will allow the selection of DESs with desired physicochemical properties in different applications and lead to further development and utilization of novel DESs as a greener alternative to organic solvents in the design and optimization of chemical and industrial processes.

Marg, Bhavnagar, 364002 Gujarat, India º Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad 201002, India ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents Physical parameters Temperature Alkyl chain length ABSTRACT In order to utilize deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as a replacement for conventional organic solvents for different applications, a detailed understanding of their physicochemical properties is extremely important. In this study, several novel DESs based on benzyl-triethylammonium chloride (BTEA) as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and acids/or alcohols as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) have been synthesized. DESs have been thoroughly characterized and investigated for their physicochemical properties viz. thermal stability, glass transition temperature, viscosity (η), surface tension (γ), refractive index (nD), density (ρ), speed of sound (u), and conductivity (κ) in a temperature range of 293.15–343.15 K. The effect of temperature, type of HBDs, and alkyl chain length of HBDs of the DESs on the physicochemical properties are critically examined and discussed. Viscosity data are fitted to Vogel-Fulcher-Tamman (VFT) and Arrhenius models. A linear model was used to fit surface tension (γ), density, refractive index, and speed of sound data whereas conductivity data were fitted to a nonlinear equation. Primary data on physicochemical properties have been used to estimate the viscous flow parameters (activation entropy, activation enthalpy, and free energy of activation) and other derived parameters such as lattice energy, standard entropy, molar volume, intermolecular free length, and isentropic compressibility. A relationship between molar conductivity and dynamic viscosity has been established to evaluate the ionicity of the synthesized DESs. Insights into the structure–property correlations are discussed in detail. ## 1. Introduction Organic solvents, which are highly combustible, poisonous, and hazardous to the environment as well as to human health, are one of the main and most frequent sources of chemicals and industrial processes. To meet the requirements of green chemistry principles, new ecologically friendly and sustainable solvents must be developed [1]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are well known for being the new adaptable, environmentally friendly, and designer solvents that can be easily created by merely combining the HBDs and HBAs in a specific molar ratio. The melting temperature of the generated liquid will be lesser than the melting points of their individual HBAs and HBDs. Abbott et al. published DESs for the very first time by mixing choline chloride (ChCl) as (HBA) and urea as (HBD) in 2003 [2]. The development of DESs depends on several interactions, including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals interaction, non-symmetricity, and mixing entropy. Even at high temperatures, several of the DESs combinations show chemical and thermal stability, with no chemical changes in their properties [3]. DESs can overcome the limitations associated with organic solvents by pos-sessing good thermal stability, low vapor pressure, non-flammability, large liquidus range, and biodegradability [4]. Although DESs are sometimes referred to as a class of ionic liquids, they differ from ionic liquids in some ways, including being less hazardous, not requiring purification, and being simpler to synthesize, which makes them easier to scale up for large-scale manufacturing [5]. DESs can have either a hydrophilic or a hydrophobic character, depending on the makeup of the constituent parts. Long-chain alkyl groups typically cause an increase in hydrophobicity. For a long time, the potential of hydrophilic DESs has been investigated in a variety of disciplines, including biomass extrac-tion, and processing, catalysis, enzyme activation, nanomaterials syn-thesis, gas separation, electrodeposition, battery technology, and pharmaceutical, etc [6–11]. When designing process equipment and scaling it up, an engineer must have a thorough understanding of thermophysical parameters connected to the solvent, such as density, viscosity, and refractive index. Pumping, mixing, and equipment size are all impacted by these characteristics, as well as mass and heat transmission. Data on thermophysical properties are also useful in choosing solvents that are appropriate for a certain procedure [15]. To better understand these characteristics of DESs, the scientific community is contributing its finest work. Accordingly, Soares et al. [16] investigated the density, viscosity, and Kamlet-Taft parameters of sodium hexanoate and decanoate-based eutectic solvents at a temperature range of 293.15–353.15 K. In the same temperature range of 293.15–343.15 K, Sánchez et al. [17] tested several additional physical characteristics, including refractive index, speed of sound, thermal expansion coefficient, isentropic-compressibility of proline and betaine-based DESs. To comprehend the fundamentals better, Achkar et al. [18] successfully wrapped up a discussion of several of these physical characteristics of DESs systems. Abbott et al. [2] measured the viscosity, refractive index, surface tension, and conductivity of [Ch]Cl: urea, and those of [Ch][Cl]: mono (phenylacetic, phenyl propionic), di (oxalic, malonic, adipic, and succinic), and tri (citric) acids [19], as well as the density, viscosity, conductivity, and surface tensions of [Ch]: ethylene glycol, glycerol, 1,4 butane diol [20]. The DESs [Ch]Cl: ethylene glycol and [Ch]Cl: glycerol, and their aqueous solutions, were measured between 298.15 and 333.15 K by Leron et al. [21] To evaluate the densities of nine distinct salts, Shahbaz et al. [22] utilized various HBAs such as methyl triphenylphosphonium, cholinium, and N-N, diethyl ethanolammonium, with numerous HBDs, including ethylene glycol, 2,2,2-trifluoroacetamide, and glycerol. It is also important to emphasize the work of Biernacki et al. [23]. They studied the type III DESs composed of xylitol, and sorbitol with choline chloride via experimental and computational approaches. In temperatures ranging from 293.15 to 353.15 K, researchers have studied the physicochemical characteristics of these DESs, including their density, viscosity, electrical conductivity, molar volume, refractive index, and molar refraction. Gardas and colleagues designed a new series of DESs by selecting benzyl tripropylammonium as HBA with lactic acid, phenol, glycerol, and ethylene glycol as HBDs. Several distinct thermodynamic parameters such as density, speed of sound, conductivity, and refractive index have been determined in the temperature range of 293.15 K–343.15 K [24]. In their expanded work reports, the same research group provide a new series of DES by replacing their previous HBA with current benzyl trimethylammonium chloride and benzyl tributylammonium chloride as HBAs with previously used HBDs. They carefully evaluated the characteristics of each DESs, such as density, sound speed, viscosity, refractive index, and electrical conductivity, and found that the molar ratio of HBD/HBA significantly affected the physicochemical characteristics of DESs in the temperature range of 283.15–343.15 K [25]. Herein, we have performed synthesis, characterization, and detailed physicochemical study of these newly synthesized DESs utilizing benzyl triethylammonium chloride (BTEA) as HBA with various organic acids (formic, acetic, butyric, valeric, pivalic, caprylic, capric, lauric, oleic, lactic, and levulinic acid) and alcohols (propane 1,2 diol, butane 1, 4 diol, and ethylene glycol) as HBDs. Investigations have been done into how several conditions, including temperature, alkyl chain length, and HBD type affect these physical properties. Physicochemical insights have been gained through precise measurements of primary physical properties such as viscosity, surface tension, refractive index, density, speed of sound, conductivity, and derived properties such as activation parameters of viscous flow (AH*, AS*, and AG*), molar volume, lattice energy, standard entropy, intermolecular free length, and isentropic compressibility as a function of temperature (293.15–343.15) at atmo- spheric pressure. Correlations of viscosity and conductivity have also been evaluated and presented. ## 2. Experimental section ### 2.1. Materials All the DESs were produced using benzyltriethyl ammonium chloride as the HBA in combination with a variety of HBDs, including propane 1,2, diol, butane 1,4 diol, ethylene glycol, lactic acid, levulinic acid, formic acid, acetic acid, butyric acid, valeric acid, pivalic acid, capric acid, caprylic acid, lauric acid, and oleic acid. Table 1 provides every detail pertaining to the substances employed in the current study. All chemical reagents were used as such without any additional sanitization. Result and discussion ### 3.1. *Thermal Stability, and glass transition temperature determination* To ascertain the thermal stability of the synthesized DESs in terms of decomposition temperature, *T*d, a thermogravimetric study was carried out. Fig. 2 shows the thermogram of newly synthesized DESs whereas the thermal stability of remaining earlier synthesized DESs is reported in our previous article [5]. Table 2 includes the associated degradation temperature for each DESs. It can be clearly observed that all the synthesized DESs show a good thermal stability range from 453.15 to 498.15 K. The observed thermal stability of DESs is showing comparable results with the previous findings [26]. Increasing chain length has been found to increase the viscosity, and DESs with higher viscosities have greater thermal stability [25]. Here, DESs with acids having comparatively smaller molecules such as BTEA: FA, BTEA: AA, BTEA: BA, BTEA: VA, and BTEA: PA has little effect on the thermal stability whereas, a significant increase in thermal stability has been observed for acids of significant chain length with increase in chain length such as BTEA: CAP (453.15 K), BTEA: CA (471.15 K), BTEA: LAU (478.15 K), and BTEA: OLE (498.15 K). Lattice energy The lattice energy is the quantity of energy necessary to change one mole of an ionic solid into its gaseous ionic components. It depends on how strongly the ions in the system interact with one another. Using equation (18), which is based on the Glasser theory [56], one might compute the lattice energies of all the synthesized DESs. The calculated lattice energy values for all the DESs were decreased with respect to the increase in temperature as shown in Fig. 10c and Table S16. The amount of charge carried by the DESs constituents and the space between them both have a significant impact on the lattice energy of a DESs combination. The distance between molecules in a lattice increases with temperature and decreases with the strength of the forces binding them together and hence, lattice energy [56]. The lattice energy is impacted by both the density and molecular weight of DESs components where density is directly proportional and molecular weight is inversely proportional to the lattice energy. Conclusions This work effectively synthesized 14 distinct DESs (including hy-drophilic as well as hydrophobic) by using benzyl triethylammonium chloride as HBA with several acids and alcohols as HBDs. Synthesized DESs are showing good thermal stability in the temperature range of 453.15–498.15 K and free-flowing ability. Physical and derived prop-erties have been analyzed as a function of temperature and structure. It has been found that as the temperature rises viscosity decreases and conductivity increases non-linearly whereas other properties such as density, surface tension, refractive index, and sound speed show a linear downward trend. The data for molar volume, intermolecular free length, isentropic compressibility, and standard entropy showed an upward trend with temperature. No appreciable variation in hardcore molecular volumes was found with the rise in temperature whereas an increase in the free volume of DESs was observed with the temperature rise. Vis-cosity measurements show the viscoelastic nature of DESs. Physical properties were also found to be significantly influenced by the change in the molecular weight/chain length of components of various DESs. The surface tension of DESs containing alcohols was higher than that of DESs based on acids, which may be related to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBA and alcohols, whereas the density of benzyl tri (alkyl) ammonium chloride-based DESs having the same HBD decreases in the order methyl > ethyl > propyl > butyl and single acid-based DESs displayed a lower density value than the double acid-based DESs. Interestingly, hydrophilic DESs are denser than water while hydrophobic DESs have lower density as compared to water. Conductivity and viscosity correlation reveals that the synthesized DESs are subionic in character wherein hydrophobic DESs are less ionic as compared to hydrophilic DESs. In a nutshell, the studies will allow the selection of DESs with desired physicochemical properties in different applications and lead to further development and utilization of novel DESs as a greener alternative to organic solvents in the design and optimization of chemical and industrial processes. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement **Kuldeep Singh**: Conceptualization, Investigation, Data curation, Formal analysis, Methodology, Writing - original draft. **Arvind Kumar**: Conceptualization, Methodology, Resources, Supervision, Data curation, Funding acquisition, Investigation, Validation, Writing - review & editing. **Declaration of Competing Interest** The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. ## Data availability The data that has been used is confidential. In this study, several novel DESs based on benzyl-triethylammonium chloride (BTEA) as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and acids/or alcohols as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) have been synthesized. DESs have been thoroughly characterized and investigated for their physicochemical properties viz. thermal stability, glass transition temperature, viscosity (η), surface tension (γ), refractive index (nD), density (ρ), speed of sound (u), and conductivity (κ) in a temperature range of 293.15–343.15 K. The effect of temperature, type of HBDs, and alkyl chain length of HBDs of the DESs on the physicochemical properties are critically examined and discussed. Viscosity data are fitted to Vogel-Fulcher-Tamman (VFT) and Arrhenius models. A linear model was used to fit surface tension (γ), density, refractive index, and speed of sound data whereas conductivity data were fitted to a nonlinear equation. Primary data on physicochemical properties have been used to estimate the viscous flow parameters (activation entropy, activation enthalpy, and free energy of activation) and other derived parameters such as lattice energy, standard entropy, molar volume, intermolecular free length, and isentropic compressibility. A relationship between molar conductivity and dynamic viscosity has been established to evaluate the ionicity of the synthesized DESs. Insights into the structure–property correlations are discussed in detail. ## 1. Introduction Organic solvents, which are highly combustible, poisonous, and hazardous to the environment as well as to human health, are one of the main and most frequent sources of chemicals and industrial processes. To meet the requirements of green chemistry principles, new ecologically friendly and sustainable solvents must be developed [1]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are well known for being the new adaptable, environmentally friendly, and designer solvents that can be easily created by merely combining the HBDs and HBAs in a specific molar ratio. The melting temperature of the generated liquid will be lesser than the melting points of their individual HBAs and HBDs. Abbott et al. published DESs for the very first time by mixing choline chloride (ChCl) as (HBA) and urea as (HBD) in 2003 [2]. The development of DESs depends on several interactions, including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals interaction, non-symmetricity, and mixing entropy. Even at high temperatures, several of the DESs combinations show chemical and thermal stability, with no chemical changes in their properties [3]. DESs can overcome the limitations associated with organic solvents by pos-sessing good thermal stability, low vapor pressure, non-flammability, large liquidus range, and biodegradability [4]. Although DESs are sometimes referred to as a class of ionic liquids, they differ from ionic liquids in some ways, including being less hazardous, not requiring purification, and being simpler to synthesize, which makes them easier to scale up for large-scale manufacturing [5]. DESs can have either a hydrophilic or a hydrophobic character, depending on the makeup of the constituent parts. Long-chain alkyl groups typically cause an increase in hydrophobicity. For a long time, the potential of hydrophilic DESs has been investigated in a variety of disciplines, including biomass extrac-tion, and processing, catalysis, enzyme activation, nanomaterials syn-thesis, gas separation, electrodeposition, battery technology, and pharmaceutical, etc [6–11]. Lattice energy The lattice energy is the quantity of energy necessary to change one mole of an ionic solid into its gaseous ionic components. It depends on how strongly the ions in the system interact with one another. Using equation (18), which is based on the Glasser theory [56], one might compute the lattice energies of all the synthesized DESs. U_POT = 1981.2(\rho/M)^{1/3} + 103.8 (18) where U_POT is the lattice energy in kJ mol⁻¹. The calculated lattice energy values for all the DESs were decreased with respect to the increase in temperature as shown in Fig. 10c and Table S16. The amount of charge carried by the DESs constituents and the space between them both have a significant impact on the lattice energy of a DESs combination. The distance between molecules in a lattice increases with temperature and decreases with the strength of the forces binding them together and hence, lattice energy [56]. The lattice energy is impacted by both the density and molecular weight of DESs components where density is directly proportional and molecular weight is inversely proportional to the lattice energy. However, the lattice energy is strongly influenced by molecular weight than density among all studied DESs as per equation (18). Additionally, comparing the lattice energy to the molar volume (according to equations (16), and 18) shows that it tends to be the reverse of the latter, with increasing molecular weight tending to increase molar volume in the former instance. Conclusions This work effectively synthesized 14 distinct DESs (including hy-drophilic as well as hydrophobic) by using benzyl triethylammonium chloride as HBA with several acids and alcohols as HBDs. Synthesized DESs are showing good thermal stability in the temperature range of 453.15–498.15 K and free-flowing ability. Physical and derived prop-erties have been analyzed as a function of temperature and structure. It has been found that as the temperature rises viscosity decreases and conductivity increases non-linearly whereas other properties such as density, surface tension, refractive index, and sound speed show a linear downward trend. The data for molar volume, intermolecular free length, isentropic compressibility, and standard entropy showed an upward trend with temperature. No appreciable variation in hardcore molecular volumes was found with the rise in temperature whereas an increase in the free volume of DESs was observed with the temperature rise. Vis-cosity measurements show the viscoelastic nature of DESs. Physical properties were also found to be significantly influenced by the change in the molecular weight/chain length of components of various DESs. The surface tension of DESs containing alcohols was higher than that of DESs based on acids, which may be related to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBA and alcohols, whereas the density of benzyl tri (alkyl) ammonium chloride-based DESs having the same HBD decreases in the order methyl > ethyl > propyl > butyl and single acid-based DESs displayed a lower density value than the double acid-based DESs. Interestingly, hydrophilic DESs are denser than water while hydrophobic DESs have lower density as compared to water. Conductivity and viscosity correlation reveals that the synthesized DESs are subionic in character wherein hydrophobic DESs are less ionic as compared to hydrophilic DESs. In a nutshell, the studies will allow the selection of DESs with desired physicochemical properties in different applications and lead to further development and utilization of novel DESs as a greener alternative to organic solvents in the design and optimization of chemical and industrial processes. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement **Kuldeep Singh**: Conceptualization, Investigation, Data curation, Formal analysis, Methodology, Writing - original draft. **Arvind Kumar**: Conceptualization, Methodology, Resources, Supervision, Data curation, Funding acquisition, Investigation, Validation, Writing - review & editing. **Declaration of Competing Interest** The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. ## Data availability The data that has been used is confidential.
